83h8qs:261: Learning abstraction costs, version drift risk, multiplied troubleshooting difficulty, and migration lock-in—these four costs are nearly inevitable in any framework-based approach. A framework essentially trades fixed structure for development efficiency, but when the domain evolves faster than the framework iterates, the framework becomes the bottleneck. Notably, the "version drift" the article points out is especially prominent in AI Agents: tool-calling protocols, multi-Agent communication patterns, and state management paradigms are all evolving rapidly. Today's framework best practices may well become technical debt in six months. Therefore, teams choosing a framework-based Agent must build their own abstraction isolation layer to keep core business logic loosely coupled with the framework implementation, thus containing migration costs when the framework must be upgraded or replaced.

pe29yd:292: The "7-question decision framework" listed in the article points to a core insight: Agent selection is essentially a matching game between organizational capability and task requirements, not a comparison game of technical superiority. A typical failure pattern is: a business owner sees that a low-code platform can quickly produce a demo and directly pushes the prototype into the production system; then, as state management complexity rises, manual confirmation points increase, and permission control becomes finer, the platform becomes increasingly unwieldy while migration costs have already grown unbearable. The root cause of this pattern is that the decision-maker silently excluded the need for "long-term control" at the "validate value" stage. The right approach is to ask clearly during the low-code stage: Will this capability become a core asset in the future? Will it need deep integration with internal systems? If the answer is unknown, it is better to use low-code to validate value first, but the architecture should reserve space for future framework migration.
prhstj:336: The path proposed in the article—"0→1 validate value, 1→10 build the skeleton, 10→100 accumulate assets"—essentially reflects an organization's learning curve for understanding AI Agent capabilities. The low-code stage addresses the question "can it be used," the framework stage addresses "can it be managed," and the in-house stage addresses "can it be controlled." These three stages are not coincidental technology choices but necessary capability steps an organization takes during AI engineering. Each step has its own complexity trap: the low-code trap is "treating a prototype as a product"; the framework trap is "mistaking learning the framework for learning Agents"; the in-house trap is "underestimating that all the infrastructure-level pain returns during the in-house stage." Understanding this explains why many teams move smoothly through low-code, then face frequent refactoring at the framework stage, and then tear everything down at the in-house stage—the root cause is that they did not complete the cognitive accumulation of the previous stage before entering the next one.
